title: Atomic Static Electric Quadrupole Polarizability from Relativistic Many-Body Theory With Application To Thulium $\left(6s^2\, 4f^{13}\right)$\, $^2F_{7/2}$ and $^2F_{5/2}$
abstract: In the present work a method for calculating atomic static electric rank-$n$ tensor quadrupole polarizabilities $α_Q^{(n)}(J)$ for arbitrary atomic electronic structure is presented. It is based on a linear-symmetry representation of atomic states using large-scale relativistic configuration interaction wavefunctions, and the quadrupole polarizabilities are obtained by a sum-over-states approach. The major result from applying this method to atomic thulium is $α_Q^{(0)}(\frac{7}{2}) = 2496^{+0}_{-231}$ \au for the electronic ground term $^2F_{7/2}$ static electric scalar quadrupole polarizability which is roughly a factor of four smaller than same property in the electronic ground state of the cesium atom. This finding adds to the favorable properties of thulium atoms in atomic-clock research.

bite.hook: Thulium's static electric scalar quadrupole polarizability is found to be 2496 atomic units.
tldr: Calculated atomic static electric rank-n tensor quadrupole polarizabilities for arbitrary electronic structures.
Used a linear-symmetry representation with large-scale relativistic configuration interaction wavefunctions and a sum-over-states approach.
Found thulium's ground term polarizability is roughly four times smaller than cesium's, favoring atomic-clock research.
bite.whyItMatters: Knowing these precise atomic properties helps researchers improve the stability and accuracy of next-generation atomic clocks.
bite.eli5: Think of measuring how easily an atom gets distorted when you put it in an electric field, kind of like squishing a tiny rubber ball. Thulium turns out to be much stiffer against this squishing than cesium, which helps scientists build better atomic clocks.
